title: Microscopic Conversion of Structural Chirality into Electronic Chirality in Artificial Chiral Clusters
abstract: We investigate how structural chirality is converted into electronic chirality in a two-dimensional cluster model consisting of a triangular-lattice core and three rod-like extensions under a surface-induced polar field.   By evaluating the electric toroidal monopole (ETM) and the Edelstein effect, we show that both quantities exhibit antisymmetric and nonmonotonic dependence   on the structural parameter controlling the cluster geometry.   While the total density of states is almost unaffected by the structural deformation, the ETM-resolved spectrum changes significantly, indicating that chirality is encoded in the symmetry character of the electronic states rather than in the overall electronic spectrum.   Real-space analysis reveals that the induced ETM is concentrated near the vertices and rods, whereas the Edelstein response extends more broadly into the core region.   Furthermore, a parameter-decomposition analysis identifies spin-orbit coupling, surface-induced parity mixing, and structural chirality as the essential ingredients for both phenomena.   Our results clarify the microscopic connection between structural chirality, electronic chirality, and chiral transport responses in artificial surface nanostructures.
summary: This paper theoretically models how structural asymmetry in artificial nanostructures can induce electronic chirality. By calculating the Electric Toroidal Monopole and the Edelstein effect, the authors demonstrate that this conversion requires the simultaneous presence of spin-orbit coupling, surface field effects, and geometric structural chirality. The findings clarify a fundamental microscopic link between structure, symmetry, and chiral transport.
main_problem: The study investigates the microscopic mechanism by which structural chirality within an artificial cluster is converted into measurable electronic chirality.
main_result: Both the Electric Toroidal Monopole (ETM) and the Edelstein effect exhibit antisymmetric dependence on structural geometry, confirming that SOC, surface-induced parity mixing, and structural chirality are essential ingredients for this chiral response.
method: The authors employed theoretical calculations involving linear response theory to evaluate transport properties and used parameter decomposition analysis to isolate the physical origins of the observed effects.
model_or_system: The model is a two-dimensional cluster composed of a triangular lattice core connected to three rod-like extensions, subjected to an external surface-induced polar field. The physics is described using an extended Hamiltonian incorporating hopping, SOC, and hybridization terms.
key_observables: Electric Toroidal Monopole (ETM), Edelstein response tensor ($\chi_{a,b}$), electrical conductivity ($\sigma_{a,b}$), and ETM-resolved density of states.
important_parameters: The structural chirality is controlled by a geometric angle $\theta$. Key physical parameters include SOC strength ($\lambda$), surface potential ($V_{sz}$), and various hopping/splitting energies.
main_assumptions: The analysis utilizes a minimal basis set (s and p orbitals) to model the effects of surface-induced parity mixing, and certain terms are omitted in parameter decomposition for clarity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the cluster geometry and $\theta$ dependence of ETM/conductivity contributions (core vs. rod), showing how chirality is encoded in state symmetry rather than total DOS. Real-space plots compare ETM and Edelstein distributions between achiral and chiral configurations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and Hamiltonian to calculating key observables (ETM, Edelstein effect). It then uses parameter decomposition analysis to microscopically identify the necessary ingredients—SOC, parity mixing, and structural chirality—that drive both electronic chirality and chiral transport responses.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical framework connecting geometric structure (structural chirality) directly to measurable quantum phenomena (electronic chirality/chiral currents), which is highly relevant for designing next-generation spintronic or topological materials.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Schematic illustration of the cluster geometry and model setup. The cluster consists of a triangular-lattice core and three rod-like extensions at- tached to its vertices. A polar ﬁeld E is present perpendicular to the cluster plane along the z direction. The angle θ, measured from the radial direction, controls the structural chirality of the cluster. The structural handedness is determined by the combination of θ and the direction of the polar ﬁeld.

Fig. 2. Structural-parameter dependence of the electric toroidal monopole (ETM) and the Edelstein response χx,x. The upper and lower panels show the ETM and χx,x, respectively. Red, green, and blue curves represent the total, core, and rod contributions. The rod contribution to χx,x is multiplied by 100 for visibility. Both quantities change sign upon reversing θ, reﬂecting the reversal of electronic chirality associated with the structural handedness.

Fig. 3. (a) Density of states (DOS) and (b) ETM-resolved DOS for rep- resentative cluster geometries at θ = 0, π/5, and 2π/5. For better visibility, the values are divided by 10−8. The horizontal solid line indicates the Fermi level at θ = π/5. In (b), DOS is projected onto the ETM operator. Although the total DOS is almost unchanged by the structural deformation, the ETM- resolved spectrum becomes ﬁnite.

Fig. 4. Real-space distributions of the site-resolved ETM and Edelstein response. Panels (a) and (c) show the onsite ETM and Edelstein response for the achiral cluster. Panels (b) and (d) show the diﬀerences from the achiral cluster for chiral clusters with (left panel) θ = π/5 and (right panel) 2π/5. We denote the onsite ETM and Edelstein response at site i in the cluster with angle θ by (G0)i[θ] and (χx,x)i[θ], for simplicity. The diﬀerence maps highlight the components induced by structural chirality.
